title: Lost and Found
logline: At a busy railway station, a counter piled with other people's things waits for owners who may never come, while a clerk decides, item by item, what honesty actually costs.
human_question: What does it cost, in the moment, to hand back something you could easily have kept?

situation.what_happens: A lost-property office receives what strangers hand in, logs it, shelves it and waits. Some things are claimed within the hour, some after months, most never. Every item on the shelf represents a decision somebody already made, quietly and without witnesses, to hand it over rather than keep it, and the clerk makes the same decision daily on a larger scale.
situation.who_is_involved: The clerk who keeps the register; the strangers who hand things in; the owners who come looking, usually certain it is gone; and the institution that eventually disposes of what nobody claims.
situation.what_is_at_stake: For an owner, sometimes a phone and sometimes a livelihood. For the clerk, a job in which temptation is a daily and unremarkable fact. For everyone watching, the plain evidence that most people, most of the time, hand it in.
situation.how_it_unfolds: Items arrive, are logged and wait out a period, then are disposed of. Reunions happen without warning and the counter never knows which day brings one. Reality decides what comes in and who turns up for it.

concept_merge.why_together: One concept. The ten unwholesome courses of action (C058) defines taking what is not given as knowing a thing belongs to another and deciding to take it anyway, and separately treats covetousness, wanting what is another's to be one's own, as an act of the mind, while distinguishing a passing wish from a settled one.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the course of action the texts describe is a decision, not a character type, and that a counter of unclaimed things is a record of thousands of people deciding the other way for no reward at all.

concept_links.why: The source defines taking what is not given by the plain fact of knowing something belongs to another and deciding to take it anyway [C058-P:L78-L86], and distinguishes a flash of wanting from a settled wish [C058-P:L239]. The counter shows the opposite decision, made quietly by strangers, over and over. The digest's warning against moralising applies: the film must not sort people into honest and dishonest, and must not present the source's claims about where an act leads as verdicts on anyone.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: The texts treat taking what is not given, and wanting what is another's, as decisions rather than dispositions, and they draw the line at the point where a passing wish settles into an intention.
what_must_be_real: A working office and its actual daily traffic; nothing is planted for the camera, and members of the public are filmed only with consent.
position_hint: middle, if it were kept: an ensemble of strangers rather than a situation with people in it over time.
risks: Filming identifiable members of the public without consent
Moralising about honest and dishonest people
Making light of a genuine loss
drop_if: No station will permit filming at the counter
The office's daily traffic is too thin to sustain a film

connections.note: Folded into the film about a family formalising inherited land, which now carries both the definition of taking what is not given and the counter-case of strangers deciding the other way.

selection.reason: Same concept as a kept idea with no slot of its own; its substance strengthens the kept idea and protects it from casting any relative as the greedy one.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
